title: Med Spa Chart Review: Co-Signing RN and NP Notes (October 2026)
summary: How med spa chart review and physician co-signing work for RN and NP notes: who must sign, how often, and how to keep the unsigned pile from growing.
body_markdown:
## What Is Med Spa Chart Review, and How Is It Different From Co-Signing?


Med spa chart review is a physician's after-the-fact check of treatment records for protocol adherence, dosing, consent and documentation quality. Co-signing is narrower: a signature on one specific note showing the physician saw it and agrees with it. Many clinics blur the two, and that blur is where gaps start.


A clinic can legitimately require either, both or neither, depending on who treated the patient. An RN working from a[standing order or patient-specific order](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-standing-orders-patient-specific-orders-explained) sits under a different regime than a nurse practitioner with a collaboration agreement. Writing down which regime applies to each person on your schedule is the first fix.


## Who Has to Co-Sign: RN, NP or PA Notes?


The treating licence and the state decide who has to co-sign. RNs generally work under physician supervision, while nurse practitioner authority ranges from fully independent to requiring a physician agreement, as the[American Association of Nurse Practitioners' state practice map](https://www.aanp.org/advocacy/state/state-practice-environment) shows.


Treating clinician What usually governs oversight Where co-signature comes from


RN Physician supervision, standing or patient-specific orders, standardized procedures in some states State supervision rules, the medical director agreement, clinic policy


Nurse practitioner Full practice authority, or a collaboration or supervision agreement Agreement terms, state rules, payer or insurer requirements


Physician assistant Delegation or supervision agreement State rules and the agreement, sometimes a percentage of charts


Physician Own licence Usually none, unless a facility requires peer review


Even where state law is silent, co-signing is often driven by policy. One EHR vendor's guide on nonphysician practitioners notes that requirements[come from practice policy, payer billing rules and clinical governance](https://www.docvilla.com/ehr/npp-nurse-practitioner-physician-assistant-cosign-requirements/) , not only from statute. A malpractice carrier may ask for it too, so read the policy you actually hold.


## What Do Regulators Expect From Supervising Physicians?


Regulators describe the expectation as active, real supervision, not a signature collected afterwards. Oklahoma's osteopathic board states in its[medical spa guidelines](https://oklahoma.gov/content/dam/ok/en/osboe/documents/guidance/Med%20Spa%20Guidelines%202-27-24.pdf) that the supervising physician "must provide timely and random chart reviews" and must actively supervise the spa. For RNs, general supervision applies, and the physician need not be in the building.


California takes a similar line from a different angle. A health-care law firm summarising the state's rules explains that[RN supervision must be real](https://cohenhealthcarelaw.com/medical-spa-laws-detail-physician-vs-nurse-authority/) , with standardized procedures and a physician who can be reached in an emergency. The same source notes that California expects a certain amount of chart review for physician assistants without giving a figure.


Both sources leave the number to you. That is deliberate: the regulators care that oversight is documented and consistent, not that you hit an arbitrary percentage. Texas is a reminder to check currency, since the state's former cosmetic procedures rule was repealed in January 2025 and older blog posts still quote it.


## How Often Should Notes Be Signed and Charts Reviewed?


Set two clocks: a signing deadline for individual notes and a review cadence for samples. A sensible starting point is 48 hours for notes on higher-risk treatments, with a monthly random sample of the rest. Many practices already use a 24 to 48 hour window to avoid billing and documentation delays, according to the same EHR guide cited above.


Which notes count as higher risk is your medical director's call. Typical candidates are first treatments for a new patient, anything involving prescription products, filler near vascular danger zones, energy devices, and any note with an adverse event. Make sure every[adverse event record](https://decodahealth.com/blog/adverse-event-reporting-med-spa) gets physician eyes regardless of the sampling rule.


A GLP-1 or hormone clinic often runs on a faster loop, because prescribing decisions depend on the note. Our guide to[screening and intake for GLP-1, TRT and peptide patients](https://decodahealth.com/blog/glp1-trt-peptide-patient-screening-intake) covers what the physician needs in front of them before a protocol is renewed.


## What Goes Wrong When Co-Signing Is a Side Task?


Co-signing fails in three predictable ways: notes pile up where nobody can see them, the physician cannot find the list, and the signature gets stamped without a read. All three show up in real support conversations with clinics.


In one recent thread a medical director who supervises a team of RNs asked how to sign a batch of notes at once. Her requirement was clear: every RN-treated chart needed her signature because her oversight is the legal basis for the treatments. What she wanted was a single filtered list, sorted by provider, location and date, that she could clear in one sitting. A list like that is the right goal for any clinic, whichever EHR you run.


The second failure is the stamped signature. A note signed in bulk without opening it satisfies a checkbox and fails the point of supervision. If your policy says "review and co-sign", the physician should be able to see the treatment record, units or settings, and photos before signing.


- **Invisible backlog:** unsigned notes sit across several screens, so the count is guesswork
- **No owner:** everyone assumes the practice manager or the physician is chasing it
- **No deadline:** a note from three weeks ago looks the same as one from this morning
- **Bulk sign without review:** the signature proves nothing about oversight


## A Weekly Routine for Med Spa Chart Review


A weekly routine beats an annual cleanup because it keeps the backlog small enough to read. Assign one person to produce the numbers and one physician to act on them. This takes under an hour for most single-location clinics.


1. **Monday:** the practice manager pulls the unsigned and awaiting-co-sign counts by provider and flags anything past 48 hours
2. **Midweek:** the physician clears the flagged notes, reading the treatment details and not just the summary
3. **Friday:** pull five to ten random charts from the week, spread across providers, and check consent, dosing, lot numbers and photos against the treatment performed
4. **Monthly:** the medical director reviews the trend, the adverse events and any note that needed correction, and records that review


Pair the sample with the[consent schedule](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-consent-forms) you set for patients. A chart where the consent on file does not match the treatment performed is the most common thing a Friday review catches.


## What Should the Medical Director Agreement Say?


The agreement should say, in plain terms, which notes get a signature, how fast, and what happens when the physician is unavailable. Vague language like "oversees clinical care" does not help the practice manager who has to run the process. Get the final text from your attorney, but bring a draft of these points.


- Which roles require a co-signature and which require only sampled review
- The signing deadline for higher-risk notes and the review cadence for the rest
- A named backup physician for vacations and illness
- How corrections and addenda are made after a note is signed
- Where evidence of review is stored, so you can produce it in an inspection


Medical oversight services exist for clinics without an in-house physician. Decoda Health's partner[WellnessMD](https://decodahealth.com/partnerships/wellness-md) provides medical director coverage, and the oversight duties above still need to be written into whatever agreement you sign. The[new med spa laws](https://decodahealth.com/blog/new-med-spa-laws) and the[inspection signals regulators look for](https://decodahealth.com/blog/ny-med-spa-sweep-compliance-signals) both put medical director involvement near the top.


## How Do You Keep Signed Notes Trustworthy?


Signed notes stay trustworthy when changes are tracked rather than overwritten. After a physician signs, any edit should create a visible addendum with the author and time, so the record shows what was signed and what changed later.


Role-based access matters here too. Front desk staff should see schedules and payments, not edit a signed clinical note, which is why we wrote a separate guide on[calendar permissions and staff roles](https://decodahealth.com/blog/decoda-calendar-permissions-staff-roles) . If your staff SOP does not yet cover who can amend what, the[staff SOP setup guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-staff-sop-setup) is a good place to add it.


## Where Does an AI Scribe Fit in Chart Review?


An AI scribe shortens the time between treatment and a finished draft, which means notes reach the signing queue the same day. It does not move responsibility: the treating clinician reviews and signs, and any physician co-signature still applies on top.


That matters for the backlog. Most of the unsigned pile comes from clinicians finishing notes at the end of a long day, and a draft that is already structured takes minutes to check. Our post on[AI scribe time savings](https://decodahealth.com/blog/ai-scribe-med-spa-time-savings) covers the numbers, and the one on[ambient documentation and dispute protection](https://decodahealth.com/blog/ai-scribe-ambient-documentation-dispute-protection) covers what a good record does for you when a patient complains.

## Final Thoughts on Med Spa Chart Review


Write the policy on one page: which roles need a co-signature, the 48-hour target for higher-risk notes, the weekly unsigned count and the monthly sample. Then run it for four weeks and see which provider's notes are always late. That conversation is usually more useful than any software setting.

## Frequently Asked Questions


Does a medical director have to co-sign every med spa chart?


Not necessarily. Whether every note needs a physician signature depends on your state's rules for the licence holder who treated the patient, any supervision or collaboration agreement, and your own policy. Some boards ask only for timely and random chart review rather than a signature on every note. Get the requirement for each role from your state board and attorney, then write it into the medical director agreement.


How often should a supervising physician review med spa charts?


There is no single national interval. Regulators in some states describe the expectation in general terms, such as timely and random chart review, and leave the schedule to the practice. A workable default is to sign higher-risk notes within 48 hours and review a random sample of the rest every month. Ask your medical director and attorney to confirm that cadence for your state.


What is the difference between chart review and co-signing a note?


Co-signing is a signature on a specific note that confirms the physician saw and agrees with it. Chart review is a broader quality check, usually a sample of charts looked at after the fact for protocol adherence, dosing and documentation. A practice can require both, only one, or neither for a given role, depending on state law and its own policy.


Do nurse practitioners need a physician to co-sign their notes?


It depends on the state and the practice. States with full practice authority generally do not require a physician signature on NP notes, while other states require a collaboration or supervision agreement that may include chart review. Payers, malpractice carriers and the practice itself can also require co-signing even when the state does not.


What should happen when a co-signature is overdue?


Treat it as a defined escalation, not a silent backlog. A common pattern is a reminder to the physician at 24 hours, a flag to the practice manager at 48 hours and a weekly count reviewed with the medical director. Record the reason for any delay, because an old unsigned note reads badly in an audit.


Can an AI scribe replace physician chart review?


No. An AI scribe drafts the note faster, but the licensed clinician who treated the patient still reviews and signs it, and the physician's oversight duties stay with the physician. Where a physician co-signature is required, the scribe only moves the note into the signing queue sooner.
